<research_package>

## Research question
Does fine-tuning on self-generated concise reasoning (Method M) shorten LLM reasoning without reducing accuracy, compared with prompting and other fine-tuning approaches, and does the effect transfer across math datasets?

## Methods summary
Method M is a self-training recipe for shorter chain-of-thought. For each training question, the model samples reasoning paths while conditioned on 8 concise few-shot exemplars (here written by GPT-4o), plus paths from its default distribution; the shortest correct path per question is kept, and the model is fine-tuned on these paths. Method M-FS samples a single few-shot-conditioned path instead of best-of-N. Baselines: zero-shot prompting (including an explicit 'be concise' instruction), fine-tuning on external reasoning (GPT-4o chain-of-thought), naive best-of-N self-training without exemplars (16 paths), and Rational Metareasoning.

## Experimental setup
Five post-trained models (Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B, Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, DeepSeekMath-7B), fine-tuned separately for GSM8K and MATH; evaluation on the GSM8K test set and MATH500 with greedy decoding. Accuracy is parsed from final answers; length is the mean number of output tokens over all outputs, correct or not. Relative metrics divide by the zero-shot baseline prompt. Method M uses 16 few-shot-conditioned plus 16 default paths per question; the budget-matched variant uses 8 plus 8.

## Experiments and comparisons
- `exp1`: Concise-reasoning methods on GSM8K and MATH (T1)
  - comparison `exp1/cmp1`: Method M vs zero-shot baseline: accuracy and output length
  - comparison `exp1/cmp2`: Method M vs other length-reduction approaches (concise prompting, FT on GPT-4o CoT, naive best-of-N, Rational Metareasoning)
  - comparison `exp1/cmp3`: Method M full-budget vs budget-matched generation
- `exp2`: Cross-task generalization (T2)
  - comparison `exp2/cmp1`: In-domain vs out-of-domain relative accuracy and length

sentences.text: Fine-tuning on self-generated concise reasoning (Method M) reduced output length more than any other approach on both datasets, to 64.25% of the zero-shot baseline on GSM8K and 76.30% on MATH, but this came with no accuracy gain: relative accuracy was 97.00% on GSM8K and 102.56% on MATH.

The length reduction transferred across datasets but was weaker out-of-domain: training on GSM8K reduced MATH length to 88.34% (vs 64.25% in-domain) and training on MATH reduced GSM8K length to 90.36% (vs 76.30% in-domain), while out-of-domain accuracy remained near baseline (99.21% and 98.53%).

Budget-matched Method M (8+8 paths) produced slightly less length reduction than the full-budget version (16+16) on both datasets (GSM8K: 67.15% vs 64.25%; MATH: 80.43% vs 76.30%) with similar relative accuracy (GSM8K: 97.44% vs 97.00%; MATH: 101.58% vs 102.56%).
No significance tests were reported, and standard deviations were large (e.g., GSM8K relative length SD 16.66 for Method M), so these differences should be interpreted cautiously.

Fine-tuning on self-generated concise reasoning (Method M) reduced output length to 64.25% of the zero-shot baseline on GSM8K and 76.30% on MATH500, with relative accuracies of 97.00% and 102.56%, respectively.

In this comparison, Method M showed the lowest relative length among the evaluated methods on both datasets (e.g., 64.25% vs. 67.60% for FT on GPT-4o CoT and 87.17% for naive best-of-N on GSM8K), but its GSM8K relative accuracy (97.00%) was numerically lower than several baselines, including the 'Be Concise' prompt (99.85%) and Method M-FS (99.94%).

The length reduction did not fully transfer across datasets: relative to the zero-shot baseline on each test set, models fine-tuned on GSM8K and tested on MATH reduced length to 88.34%, and models fine-tuned on MATH and tested on GSM8K reduced length to 90.36%, compared with in-domain reductions of 64.25% and 76.30%, respectively.
No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in accuracy and length cannot be interpreted as statistically significant or reliable.

Fine-tuning on self-generated concise reasoning (Method M) reduced output length to 64.25% of the zero-shot baseline on GSM8K and 76.30% on MATH500, while maintaining accuracy within 3 percentage points of the baseline on both datasets (97.00% and 102.56% relative accuracy, respectively).

Compared with other length-reduction approaches, Method M achieved the largest length reduction on both datasets (e.g., 64.25% vs. 67.60% for FT on GPT-4o CoT and 87.17% for naive best-of-N on GSM8K), with comparable or better relative accuracy than these baselines.

The length reduction from Method M did not fully transfer across datasets: models fine-tuned on GSM8K and tested on MATH reduced length to 88.34% of baseline, and models fine-tuned on MATH and tested on GSM8K reduced length to 90.36%, compared with in-domain reductions of 64.25% and 76.30%, respectively.
No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in accuracy and length cannot be interpreted as statistically significant or reliable.
